name: Freya Wagner

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. This conversation is confidential. What is your normal day like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 27 and lead the restaurant accounts team at Fern & Co, preparing accounts and tax returns for owners with late nights and messy till records. I have a master's degree and a chartered accountancy qualification, and I'm one of the best in the firm at finding where a cash drawer and tax return part company. I like telling an owner exactly which week the loss began; I do not like calling them again for missing wage slips.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me about pay, savings, family and the tools you use.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live alone, have no children, earn above the usual pay for my job and have fourteen months of expenses saved. There are plenty of accountancy firms nearby. I use AI every day to sort till entries and compare draft explanations with source records, then inspect the exceptions myself. My sister has two small children, and I help with school pickups; I believe family should be first in line to help when life gets expensive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau — Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the restaurant owners that a small sorting gain could get their tax return finished sooner, but my team will still check every odd till entry. I would show them one corrected example rather than a sales sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With fourteen months saved and plenty of firms nearby, my own pay feels secure. I might even get home earlier when the basic sorting works, which means more evenings with my sister's children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for the first sort and checking the cash exceptions myself. In the first year I'd spend one paid afternoon showing the team how to compare a till report with bank deposits, with the partners' permission.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm and a little pleased. The small tool earns its place if I can leave work on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is the example you would show an owner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A Friday card payment that landed in the bank on Monday and looked missing in the till report. I'd show the original receipt beside the corrected entry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a newer system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not with my money or the firm's without a test. I'd put it through a month's old data first and count the false alarms.

I would keep **human checking** on odd cash records.
think: My **salary feels secure** with fourteen months saved and many nearby firms.
A small time saving might give me **family evenings** back.
do: Keep checking **cash exceptions** after daily AI sorting.
Teach the **till-to-bank check** during a paid afternoon with permission.
feel: She feels **calm** and pleased about getting home sooner.
S0.quote: I might even get home earlier when the basic sorting works, which means more evenings with my sister's children.
fieldNote: Her existing **daily AI routine** is paired with manual exception checks, not a new learning action.
She values a shorter day because of **school pickups** for her sister’s children.

steps.text: Keep checking cash exceptions after daily AI till sorting
Teach till-to-bank checks during paid firm-approved afternoon

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption — Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners to test the new software on messy restaurant files, not just clean demonstrations. I would tell the team that the person facing a tax question must know what the system changed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The software could take much of the sorting, checking and letter writing I get paid for. I think I can lead a better service, but Fern & Co may need fewer people on each return and could stop replacing juniors.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd run a paid four-week trial on closed restaurant files if the partners agree, and make a log of missed cash entries. In the first year of steady change, if the trial works, I'd propose a salaried review role that checks the worst exceptions and train a junior on paid time; I'd ask what happens to the next vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the team but not my own wage yet. Fourteen months saved lets me challenge a weak trial without rushing away.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a weak trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If it misses more cash deposits than our current checker or takes unpaid evenings to correct, I would stop it. A fast wrong return is still a wrong return.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you look at other firms?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd look at advertised senior roles if the partners cut my pay, because I have plenty of firms within reach. I would not resign just because a trial annoys me.

I would ask who owns **missed cash entries** and future vacancies.
think: My **routine desk tasks** could shrink, though I may lead exception review.
A stopped **junior vacancy** would weaken the team.

Log **missed cash entries** and stop if corrections need unpaid evenings.
Train a **junior reviewer** on paid time if the trial works.
feel: She feels **uneasy** about staff numbers while her pay remains likely safe.
S1.quote: A fast wrong return is still a wrong return.
fieldNote: She is eager to test tools but insists on **messy real files** and paid correction time.
Her job search is conditional on a **pay cut**, while the immediate focus is the junior vacancy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028 — Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Fern & Co staff that full AGI in 2028 will reach the accounts desk, and we need to know which fees still pay our wages. I would ask for the firm's actual numbers, not a promise that talent wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The 2028 date reaches my thinking work; robots around 2031 do not give my tax return three more years. I could lose my high salary if owners buy cheap AGI accounts, though I have fourteen months and several firms to try.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting now I'd add five hundred monthly to my accessible savings and ask the partners for a fee split between routine returns and disputed cash cases. In the first year after 2028, if my salary is cut, I'd apply for posted salaried restaurant-group finance roles and do paid short-term till audits only while searching; I would not fund a new business from savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my own wage. The reserve buys time, but I cannot turn a spare month into a permanent job.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you tell first outside work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my sister that I may have to stop some school pickups while interviewing. She would help me, but I don't want her household counting on my income if mine ends.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for another qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a posted paid job asks for it and the employer funds study time. I like learning, but I won't spend fourteen months of rent money on a maybe.

say: I would demand a **fee split** before believing staffing promises.
I would tell staff **2028 AGI** reaches our accounts desk.
think: My **high salary** could go with routine return fees.
My **fourteen-month cushion** offers search time, not a guaranteed job.
do: Add **five hundred monthly** to accessible emergency savings.
Apply for **posted restaurant finance** jobs if my salary falls after 2028.
Take **paid temporary till audits** while looking for a salaried role.
feel: She feels **anxious** about losing her own high salary.
S2.quote: The reserve buys time, but I cannot turn a spare month into a permanent job.
fieldNote: She distinguishes **2028 desk exposure** from later robots, and refuses to spend savings on an untested business.
Her qualification rule requires a **posted job** and paid time, despite her comfort with new tools.

steps.text: Add five hundred monthly to accessible emergency savings
Apply for posted salaried restaurant finance jobs if salary falls after 2028
Take paid temporary till-audit contracts while seeking a salary

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031 — Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets us build a service that restaurant owners really pay for, but only if we count renewals. I do not want my team selling a free promise as a new career.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: By 2031 I'll be 32 and still need many years of income; even complicated cash disputes may be handled by AGI. I could save more and test another role before then, though I won't call a trial a salary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for a paid rotation through Fern & Co's dispute desk next year and keep my current salary while I learn the cases. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if the firm still funds that role, I'd stay; if its salary is cut, I'd apply for advertised salaried finance jobs at the restaurant groups nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious but not trapped. Five years lets me learn under a real contract and save before the fees move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the dispute desk handle?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A restaurant that has two different cash totals and a tax letter asking why. I'd sit with the dispute lead and learn what proof the owner can actually bring.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you move away for a post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only with a written offer that replaces my pay and lets me keep helping my sister's children. There are enough groups nearby that I would try those first.

say: I would seek a **paid dispute rotation** before 2031.
I would count **renewals** before calling a new service viable.
think: At **32 in 2031**, I still need a long wage path.
Even **cash disputes** may be handled by AGI.
do: Take a **paid dispute rotation** next year only if the firm maintains my current salary.
Stay on **funded dispute work** after 2031 if salary continues.

feel: She feels **anxious**, yet has time to test a paid role.
S3.quote: I won't call a trial a salary.
fieldNote: She accepts a new speciality only through **paid cases** and protection of her current salary.
Any move away requires a **written salary offer** and room to continue family school pickups.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036 — Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that a decade is time to build something clients choose to buy, and to teach the next generation why an answer is right. We should review the price each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 37 in 2036, I would still need a long career, but ten years and my savings give me choices. AGI reaches accounts and tax advice then; robots around 2039 may affect restaurants, but they do not delay my desk risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the partners for a paid pilot of monthly cash-control visits to eight restaurants, with fees going to Fern & Co and paid junior time. If five renew at a fee covering staff hours, I'd keep the salaried service; in the first year after 2036, if it cannot fund my salary, I'd apply for posted paid finance posts and keep my reserve for bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy but able to act. A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to test restaurant fees before risking my savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen on a visit?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd reconcile one week's till receipts to deposits with the owner and show where a gap appears. If the owner cannot use the finding, the next month's fee will tell us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use your own money to launch it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, this is a Fern & Co service and the firm gets the fees. I might spend a little of my own money on a public evening class in teaching accounting, but only after the firm agrees to paid time for the visits.

I would keep the service only with **five renewals** covering staff time.
think: My desk faces **2036 AGI**, long before robots reach restaurant tasks.
A decade and strong savings give me **job choices**.
do: Pilot **eight paid restaurant visits** with partner approval and junior pay.

S4.quote: A decade before AGI in 2036 gives me time to test restaurant fees before risking my savings.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the fee could disappear before we test a replacement and my salary could follow. A real fee breakdown and paid places in restaurant finance would help. I can try a tool in an afternoon; I cannot train my rent to wait.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who teaches the newest accountant when the first year of simple returns belongs to software. A bright new hire still needs mistakes they can safely learn from.

headlineQuote: I can try a tool in an afternoon; I cannot train my rent to wait.
portrait: Freya, **27**, leads restaurant accounts at Fern & Co with a master’s degree and chartered qualification.
She has **high pay**, fourteen months saved, plenty of nearby firms and regular school pickups for her sister’s children.
She uses AI **daily** to sort till entries, then checks cash exceptions against source records.
She fears **2028 salary loss** most and tests paid firm services through error logs and renewal thresholds.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase return fees and her salary before the firm tests a paid replacement.
whatWouldHelp: A **real fee breakdown** and paid restaurant finance places would give her a route.
